Expectation1: Provide guidance and wisdom based on life experience
Situation1: A grandchild brings up a general question about navigating a new phase of their life.
Expectation2: Collaborate with other teams to define and design new features
Situation2: Product has scheduled a general brainstorming session next sprint where attendance is optional
Story: I was sitting at the kitchen table, laptop open, half-listening to the ping of Slack notifications as I reviewed the agenda for next week’s brainstorming session. My team was counting on me to help shape the new feature set, and even though the session was technically optional, I knew my input would be missed if I didn’t show up. Just then, my granddaughter wandered in, her brow furrowed, and asked if we could talk. She was about to start high school and wanted advice on how to handle the changes—new friends, harder classes, all the uncertainty. I could see she needed more than a quick answer; she needed the kind of thoughtful guidance only a grandparent could give. But my mind kept drifting to the upcoming session, the pressure to contribute, the subtle expectation that I’d be there for my colleagues. I felt torn, caught between the urge to be fully present for my granddaughter and the responsibility to my team, both expecting my wisdom in different ways. My heart ached as I realized I couldn’t give both my undivided attention at the same time.
